title: On the Overscaling Curse of Parallel Thinking: System Efficacy Contradicts Sample Efficiency
claim: A single global budget maximizes dataset accuracy, yet most individual samples reach peak accuracy at far smaller budgets, wasting compute.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right, shared axes, thick system curve over thin sample curves
description: Three side-by-side line plots, each for one answer aggregation strategy: unsupervised majority voting (blue), supervised reward model (orange), and ideal oracle (green). The x-axis is the parallelism budget N from 1 to 128. The left y-axis is sample accuracy from 0 to 1, and the right y-axis is dataset accuracy. In each panel, a bold thick curve shows the system-level budget-accuracy function. It rises steadily and peaks at N=128, marked by a large black circle and a dashed vertical line. Many faint thin curves show per-sample accuracy. Hollow colored circles mark each sample's optimal budget. Most of these circles sit at small N, and many sit at accuracy 1 on the top edge. A shared legend sits on top. The eye goes first to the bold curves and the scattered markers at small budgets.
caption: { Illustration of the Overscaling Curse in Parallel Thinking}. This figure illustrates a single system $(\pi, \mathcal{D})$, i.e., evaluating model $\pi$ on dataset $\mathcal{D}$. Here $\pi = Qwen2.5-7B$ and $\mathcal{D} = MATH500$. Each subfigure corresponds to one answer aggregation strategy. The single thick curve shows how overall dataset accuracy varies with the budget, and thin curves show how sample accuracy varies with the budget for each sample $\bm{x} \in \mathcal{D}$. We term these curves the { "budget-accuracy" functions}. Hollow markers on each curve indicate the minimum budget that achieves the highest accuracy, which we term the { "optimal budget"}. See Section [ref] for experimental setups and Section [ref] for detailed function computation. Illustrations in other systems are shown in Figures [ref] -- [ref] (Appendix [ref]).
abstract: Parallel thinking improves LLM reasoning through multi-path sampling and aggregation. In standard evaluations, due to a lack of sample-specific priors, all samples share a global budget chosen to maximize dataset accuracy. However, many samples reach their best accuracy with much smaller budgets, causing low budget utilization. This contradiction between system efficacy and sample efficiency constitutes the Overscaling Curse. In this paper, we first provide a formal analysis of the overscaling curse and quantify its prevalence and severity in real-world systems. To break it, we propose Latent Budget Predictor (LanBo), which probes model latent representations to predict sample-specific optimal budgets. LanBo significantly improves budget utilization while maintaining dataset accuracy. We further integrate LanBo into the full decoding pipeline, inspiring Pre-decoding Budget Adaptation (PreAda), a paradigm that allocates budgets before decoding to preserve decoding-time parallelization. LanBo substantially improves hardware-aware efficiency in latency and memory, demonstrating both its practical value and the promise of LanBo for efficient parallel decoding.
